facts.fact_text: On Sunday 6 September 2015, another opposition political party organised a large anti-government rally in the central square of Chișinău.
The applicants participated in the large anti-government rally held on 6 September 2015 in the central square of Chișinău.
Other sympathisers of the party 'Casa noastră - Moldova' (Our home – Moldova) participated in the large anti-government rally held on 6 September 2015 in the central square of Chișinău.
Immediately after the rally, a large group of persons led by the applicants marched towards the headquarters of the Prosecutor General's Office to demand the Prosecutor General's resignation.
At approximately 2.15 p.m. on 6 September 2015, the group approached the building of the Prosecutor General's Office.

A video of the event, which is part of the case-file, shows several members of the group wearing black t-shirts with the inscription ПЛХ-ПНХ (the abbreviation in Russian of the words meaning 'Fuck you Plahotniuc') rushing on the steps of the Prosecutor General's Office building towards its entrance.

In the video of the event, the fifth applicant can be seen approaching one of the entrance doors of the Prosecutor General's Office building and sitting right next to it while leaning against the door.
Many more members of the group climbed the steps of the Prosecutor General's Office building and rushed towards the entrance doors, being stopped and pushed back by police officers.
No violence is seen on the video footage apart from the pushing of the demonstrators by the police officers away from the entrance of the Prosecutor General's Office building.

The demonstrators were seen on the video footage shouting slogans including 'Rușine' (meaning 'Shame on you'), 'Plahotniuc la dubă' (meaning 'Plahotniuc in prison') and 'Jos mafia' ('Down with the mafia').
The demonstrators were seen on the video footage whistling and drum beating.
The majority of the demonstrators stayed on the pavement, the lawn and the road in front of the Prosecutor General's Office building, with only several dozen being on the lower part of the steps.

After being pushed to the lower part of the stairs, at approximately 2.18 p.m. on 6 September 2015, a group of approximately 15-20 demonstrators, including the applicants, sat on the steps at the feet of the police cordon.

The group of approximately 15-20 demonstrators, including the applicants, announced at approximately 2.18 p.m. that they intended to install tents and stay at the Prosecutor General's Office until the resignation of the Prosecutor General.
At 2.27 p.m. on 6 September 2015, several demonstrators started installing tents on the pavement in front of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
Having been pushed to the pavement, the demonstrators again sat down at approximately 2.31 p.m. on 6 September 2015, this time on the pavement in front of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
At 4.01 p.m. on 6 September 2015, many demonstrators were scattered on the pavement, lawn and road in front of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
At 4.01 p.m. on 6 September 2015, approximately ten tents were installed on the sidewalk in front of the steps of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
A group of demonstrators including some of the applicants were seen seated on the lower part of the steps of the Prosecutor General's Office building.

The first applicant shouted through a megaphone that the demonstration at the Prosecutor General's Office was a peaceful demonstration and that they had the constitutional right to peacefully protest.

Judge S.B. stated in her dissenting opinion that after having viewed the video footage included in the case-file and having examined the other materials of the case, she did not find any evidence of violence against the police during the demonstration of 6 September 2015.
Judge S.B. stated in her dissenting opinion that she saw a peaceful gathering of persons protesting against the Government and expressing their discontent with the policy of the Government.
Several police officers immediately lifted the fifth applicant up and pushed him away from the entrance of the Prosecutor General's Office building.

Within two to three minutes, the demonstrators were pushed away from the entrance doors of the Prosecutor General's Office building towards the lower part of the steps by a group of policemen who outnumbered them.
At 2.29 p.m. on 6 September 2015, the police forces started pushing the demonstrators further away from the entrance of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
At 4.42 p.m. on 6 September 2015, members of the special forces and the police started taking away the tents from the pavement in front of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
In spite of some protesters' attempts to retain the tents, within two minutes all tents were taken away by the police from the pavement in front of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
At 4.47 p.m. on 6 September 2015, all the demonstrators were pushed away from both the steps, the pavement and the lawn in front of the Prosecutor General's Office building.
All the applicants were arrested at approximately 4.39 p.m. on 6 September 2015.
All the applicants were taken to a police station following their arrest on 6 September 2015.

The applicants were placed in detention for a period of seventy-two hours on suspicion of having committed the offence of participating in mass disorders provided for by Article 285 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova.
On 8 September 2015, the applicants were formally charged with the offence of participating in mass disorders under Article 285 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova.
On 8 September 2015, the Rîşcani District Court ordered the applicants' remand in custody for a period of thirty days.
The applicants' detention was prolonged several times after the initial thirty-day remand in custody.
On 22 February 2016, the Rîşcani District Court ordered the applicants' house arrest.
While under house arrest, the applicants were obliged to wear electronic bracelets.

On 26 April 2016, the court ordered as one of many surety measures in respect of the applicants other than the fourth applicant the prohibition on participating in public gatherings, if there was a risk of the gathering degenerating into mass disorders.
The prohibition on participating in public gatherings imposed on 26 April 2016 was prolonged on many occasions by the Rîşcani District Court.

On 28 June 2017, the Rîşcani District Court found the applicants guilty as charged with the offence of participating in mass disorders under Article 285 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova.
On 28 June 2017, the Rîşcani District Court sentenced the applicants to suspended sentences of three and four years' imprisonment.

Article 285(1) of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Mass disorders', as in force at the material time, provided that organizing or leading mass disorders involving violence against persons, pogroms, arson, damage to goods, the use of firearms or other objects used as weapons, and violent or armed resistance to representatives of authorities shall be punished by imprisonment for 4 to 8 years.

Article 285(2) of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Mass disorders', as in force at the material time, provided that active participation in the commission of actions set forth in Article 285(1) shall be punished by imprisonment for 3 to 7 years.

Article 285(3) of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Mass disorders', as in force at the material time, provided that calls for active, violent insubordination to the legitimate requests of the authorities' representatives, and for participation in mass disorders and for the commission of acts of violence against persons shall be punished by a fine in the amount of 200 to 500 conventional units or by community service for 180 to 240 hours or by imprisonment for up to 2 years.

Article 191(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Provisional release under judicial control', as in force at the material time, provided that the provisional release under judicial control of a person under preventive arrest, of a detainee or of a person in whose case an arrest request was filed, may be granted by the investigative judge or, as the case may be, the court and shall imply one or several of the obligations set forth in Article 191(3).

Article 191(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Provisional release under judicial control', as in force at the material time, provided that provisional release under judicial control shall not be granted to a suspect/accused/defendant if he/she has convictions which remain in the criminal record for serious, especially serious or exceptionally serious crimes or if there are indications that he/she will commit another crime, will try to influence witnesses, will destroy sources of evidence or will evade justice.

Article 191(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Provisional release under judicial control', as in force at the material time, provided that the provisional release under judicial control of an arrestee shall imply one or several obligations, including: not to leave the place of domicile other than under the conditions set by the investigative judge or court; to notify the criminal investigative body or court about any change of domicile; not to appear in specifically determined places; to appear whenever summoned by the criminal investigative body or court; not to contact specific persons; not to commit any actions preventing the finding of the truth in criminal proceedings; not to drive vehicles or not to practise a profession used in the commission of the crime; and to leave the passport with the investigating judge or the court.

Article 191(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Provisional release under judicial control', as in force at the material time, provided that the police in the territorial jurisdiction in which a suspect/accused/defendant temporarily released lives shall exert control over him/her meeting the obligations set by the court.

Article 191(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Moldova, entitled 'Provisional release under judicial control', as in force at the material time, provided that judicial control over a temporarily released person may be cancelled, wholly or partially, for justifiable reasons and in the manner set for this measure.

In their appeal against the remand in custody decision, the applicants argued that there was not one single piece of evidence confirming the alleged violence against the police during the demonstration of 6 September 2015.

In their appeal against the remand in custody decision, the applicants indicated that there were no medical documents supporting the accusation about violence against the police during the demonstration of 6 September 2015.

Judge S.B. stated in her dissenting opinion that she saw a peaceful gathering of persons protesting against the Government and expressing their discontent with the policy of the Government.
Judge S.B. stated in her dissenting opinion that the demonstration of 6 September 2015 had taken place on a Sunday and had not hindered in any way the work of the Prosecutor General's Office.

The Supreme Court of Justice found that the applicants' conviction had been based exclusively on the interpretation and description of the facts made by the prosecution without any attention having been paid to the position of the applicants and to the materials of the case-file.
